messages.author: 63023c771a070260
messages.subject: rmr2 2.2.0 available
parts:
From the Changelog:

  • equijoin now accepts I/O format specs like mapreduce.
  • rmr.options now give access to a dfs.tempdir setting to set the HDFS tempdir to a different setting from the R tempdir.
  • rmr.str returns its own argument, which allows less intrusive code changes when adding logging.
  • Made some error messages more informative.
  • Bugs affecting c.keyval, equijoin, keyval, the CSV input and ouput formats, the "reduce calls" counter and the backend.parameters option to mapreduce
 Nice to see so many features driven by customer feedback (all but one), some running rmr2 in production. Bugs also seem to follow from people stressing rmr2 in new and unexpected ways, more than some fundamental flaw. Enjoy and please let the feedback flow, here on the issue tracker or the New York Times (the latter if positive).


Antonio

Not that I know of. You'll forgive me for the little hyperbole. The idea is that spreading the word about what RHadoop is good for and do it from your independent venue and with the level of detail you and your organization are OK with helps the project very much. Sometimes people file bug reports but once the problems are worked out they go silent, that's of course well within their rights. But if you have a moment to write a report about your experience with RHadoop, that's very helpful. What helps more than "This thing is AWESOME! OMG!", albeit full  of youthful enthusiasm, is "I had this problem, I solved it with the help of RHadoop, it worked". My favorite is to see code examples, but it doesn't have to go to that level of detail. Of course you have have been a great advocate already, thanks a lot.

messages.author: 03290ff051991093
messages.subject: Re: [RHadoop:#744] Re: rmr2 2.2.0 available
parts:
Actually, I think you have done a wonderful job integrating Hadoop with R. They key point is that everything is very R-like, so that you can wrap MapReduce jobs into function calls, then pass the results to other functions, loop around them, and so forth. Essentially one does not have the feeling that one is doing something outside of R, while in fact one is working with Hadoop behind the scenes, which is obviously quite different than R. So to integrate all of this together, and do it in an elegant way is a remarkable feat.

Also, the local backend is incredibly useful. This is for two reasons. First, you can debug your MapReduce code with so much ease, it's almost frightening. In particular, to insert select calls to browser in the mapper or reducer worlks wonders; not only for debugging, but also for writing new code. In particular, it makes it very easy to see what's going on inside the mapper and reducer. Without the local backend, it would be a lot more difficult, since the mapper and reducer would not be running "inside R," but in a separate process. The second reason is that it's much faster to use the local backend. When submitting a job to Hadoop, it always takes a few seconds until it even starts running, and then again a few seconds until everything is cleand up after the job finishes. In contrast, with the local backend, it reacts instantaneously, which makes it much faster to improve your code. Of course, with the local backend, one can only use it on small example data, but that's completely OK, since once the program works on the small example data set, it is relatively easy to switch back to the Hadoop backend and run it on the big data.

To give you an example how easy it is to use RHadoop, my team and I have created a relatively large project using Hadoop Streaming and R. It took months to get it running properly, since so many details had to be explicitly taken care of. (The long duration to write the code might also have been a function of our inexperience with Hadoop.) But I found it shocking that I was able to re-implement a large portion of that project in RHadoop (in particular rmr) over the last few days. So what once took us months to write was possible to be rewritten in days using RHadoop. (Again, this might to some extent be a function of us being now more experienced with Hadoop, but I don't think tha'ts the whole story and that still rmr is much nicer to work with).

I also find it very encouraging that Antonio is always very responsive. The minor problems I had so far with RHadoop led to two issues on the issue tracker, and both of them were fixed within a matter of hours.

To sum it up: many congratulations on writing such an outstanding piece of software, and keep up the good work!
